topics.title: Map skills: six-figure grid references, contours and bearings
topics.intro: Ordnance Survey maps reward precision. A six-figure grid reference pins a place to within 100 metres; contours show the shape of the land; bearings give an exact direction.
topics.teach: Explain how to give a six-figure grid reference, and why eastings come first.
topics.talk: Plan a walk together on an OS map (or the OS app) and ask {her} to read the contours along the route.

topics.title: Plate tectonics
topics.intro: The Earth’s crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year. What happens at their edges builds mountains, opens oceans and shakes cities. The Greeks blamed Poseidon, the Earth-shaker; we have better evidence.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a destructive and a constructive plate boundary, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why Iceland is getting wider every year.

topics.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes: case studies
topics.intro: The same size of earthquake can kill a hundred people in one country and a hundred thousand in another. Case studies show why: wealth, buildings, planning and luck.
topics.teach: Explain why the 2010 Haiti earthquake killed far more people than many larger earthquakes in richer countries.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what happened to the island of Thera (Santorini) about 3,600 years ago.

topics.title: Weather, pressure and rainfall
topics.intro: Weather is what is happening in the sky today; climate is the pattern over thirty years or more. Air pressure, the ocean and the shape of the land explain most of what the UK gets.
topics.teach: Explain the three types of rainfall, with a place where each is common.
topics.talk: Watch a weather forecast together and ask {her} to spot a depression (a low) and a high.

topics.title: Climate change: causes, effects and responses
topics.intro: The climate has always changed, but never this fast in human history. Separate the evidence, the natural causes, the human causes and the choices we can still make.
topics.teach: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect in four steps.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which response to climate change {she} thinks matters most: changing energy, food, transport or something else.

topics.title: Rivers and flooding
topics.intro: A river shapes its valley from source to mouth: erosion in the hills, meanders in the middle course, floodplains and deltas near the sea. Floods are natural; the damage depends on what we build.
topics.teach: Explain how an oxbow lake forms, in four steps.
topics.talk: On a walk by a river, ask {her} to find the fastest-flowing side of a bend.

topics.title: Coasts: erosion, landforms and management
topics.intro: Waves attack the coast with hydraulic action and abrasion, carry sand along it by longshore drift, and build it back as beaches and spits. Deciding what to protect is a hard choice.
topics.teach: Explain how a headland becomes a stack and then a stump.
topics.talk: Ask {her} whether the government should protect every stretch of eroding coast, and why.

topics.title: Glaciers and the shape of upland Britain
topics.intro: Twenty thousand years ago ice covered most of Britain. The Lake District, Snowdonia and the Highlands are still shaped by it: corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys and ribbon lakes.
topics.teach: Explain how a corrie forms.
topics.talk: Look at a photo of Striding Edge or Windermere together and ask {her} to name the glacial landform.

topics.title: Ecosystems and biomes
topics.intro: A biome is a huge ecosystem shaped by climate: rainforest, hot desert, tundra. Each has plants and animals adapted to it, and each faces its own threats.
topics.teach: Explain why tropical rainforest soils are poor even though the forest is so lush.
topics.talk: Ask {her} for three ways a camel or a cactus is adapted to the desert.

topics.title: Population and migration
topics.intro: There are now about 8 billion people. Why do some countries grow fast while others shrink? And why do people move?
topics.teach: Explain the five stages of the demographic transition model.
topics.talk: Ask {her} for one push factor and one pull factor in a family or local migration story you know.

topics.title: Urbanisation and megacities
topics.intro: Since about 2007 more people have lived in towns and cities than in the countryside. Megacities such as Lagos and Mumbai grow by millions in a decade; London grew the same way 150 years ago.
topics.teach: Explain the opportunities and challenges of living in a fast-growing city such as Lagos.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what an informal settlement is, and why it is a mistake to call it just a slum.

topics.title: Development and inequality
topics.intro: How do we compare countries fairly? Income alone hides too much, so geographers use measures like the Human Development Index, and ask why gaps open and how they close.
topics.teach: Explain why HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per head alone.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what the Brandt line was, and whether it still works today.

topics.title: Globalisation and trade
topics.intro: Your phone was designed in one country, assembled in another from parts made in a dozen more. Containers, the internet and transnational companies tie the world together, for better and worse.
topics.teach: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages of a transnational company opening a factory in a lower-income country.
topics.talk: Check the labels on three things at home and ask {her} to map where they were made.

topics.title: Resources and energy
topics.intro: Food, water and energy are unevenly shared. The big question for this generation: how to power the world without wrecking the climate.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy, with two examples of each.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which renewable source suits your area best, and why.

topics.title: Regional study: Russia
topics.intro: The largest country on Earth spans two continents, eleven time zones and every cold biome from steppe to tundra. Its geography explains much of its history.
topics.teach: Explain how permafrost affects building and living in Siberia.
topics.talk: Ask {her} how long the Trans-Siberian Railway is, and how long the journey takes.

topics.title: World places: countries and capitals
topics.intro: Beyond the obvious: thirty countries every well-informed person should be able to find, and their capitals (several of which are not the biggest city).
topics.teach: Name three countries whose capital is not their largest city.
topics.talk: When a country is in the news, ask {her} to find it on a map and name its capital.

topics.title: Greece and the Mediterranean
topics.intro: The world of the Greek myths is a real landscape: mountains, thousands of islands, earthquakes and volcanoes, and a climate of hot, dry summers. Mira and Theo are island-hopping across the Aegean.
topics.teach: Explain why Greece has so many earthquakes.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which Greek island {she} would visit first, and what landform {she} would see there.

topics.title: Managing hazards (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: We cannot stop earthquakes or eruptions, but we can predict, protect and prepare. GCSE questions ask you to compare how places at different levels of development respond.
topics.teach: Explain the three Ps of hazard management with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what is in an earthquake kit in Japan, and why schools practise drills.

topics.title: Numbers in geography (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: GCSE geography expects real statistics: mean, median, mode, range and interquartile range, plus reading graphs and spotting correlation.
topics.teach: Explain why the median can describe rainfall data better than the mean.
topics.talk: Give {her} five daily temperatures and ask for the median and the range.

topics.title: The water cycle and drainage basins (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: A drainage basin is a system of inputs, stores, flows and outputs. Storm hydrographs show how quickly rain reaches the river, which is the key to understanding floods.
topics.teach: Explain why an urban drainage basin floods faster than a forested one.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what “lag time” means on a storm hydrograph.

items.prompt: In a grid reference, which comes first?

options.text: Eastings, read along the bottom
Northings, read up the side of the map
options.feedback: “Along the corridor, then up the stairs”: eastings first.

options.text: Whichever line is nearer the place
options.feedback: No: always eastings first, or you end up somewhere else entirely.

items.explain: Along the corridor (eastings), then up the stairs (northings).

items.prompt: A church is in the square with easting 34 and northing 56. It is 7 tenths of the way across and 2 tenths of the way up. What is its six-figure grid reference?

options.feedback: Write the easting with its tenth (347), then the northing with its tenth (562).
Eastings first.
That is the four-figure reference for the square; six figures add the tenths.

items.explain: Easting 34 + 7 tenths = 347; northing 56 + 2 tenths = 562. So 347562.

items.prompt: On a 1:25 000 or 1:50 000 OS map, a six-figure grid reference locates a point to within how many metres?
items.explain: Grid squares are 1 km; tenths of a square are 100 m.

items.prompt: Contour lines on a map are very close together. What does that tell you?

options.text: The slope is steep
The land is flat
options.feedback: Flat land has contours far apart, or none at all.

options.text: There is a river
options.feedback: Rivers are blue lines. Close contours show steepness.

options.text: It is a forest
options.feedback: Woodland has its own green symbol.

items.explain: Each contour joins points of equal height. Close together means the height changes quickly over a short distance.

items.prompt: On a 1:50 000 map, how many centimetres represent 1 kilometre?
What is the bearing of due east?
items.explain: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, always with three figures: north 000°, east 090°, south 180°, west 270°.

items.prompt: What is the bearing of south-west?
items.explain: South is 180°; south-west is halfway on to west (270°): 225°.

items.prompt: On an OS map, what does a small blue triangle with a dot in the middle show?

options.text: A trig point on a hilltop
A campsite with toilets and water
options.feedback: Campsites have a tent symbol.

options.text: A church with a tower or spire
options.feedback: Churches are shown by a black square or circle with a cross.

options.text: A youth hostel or mountain hut
options.feedback: Hostels have a red triangle symbol.

items.explain: Trig points are concrete pillars on hilltops, once used to survey Britain.

items.prompt: What is a spot height?

options.text: An exact height in metres, marked by a dot
The highest point shown on that map sheet
options.feedback: Spot heights appear all over a map.

options.text: A viewpoint with a wide view of the land
options.feedback: Viewpoints have their own symbol; a spot height is a number beside a dot.

items.explain: Spot heights fill in detail between contour lines.

items.prompt: What is the thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth called?
items.explain: Continental crust is about 30–50 km thick; oceanic crust only about 7 km.

items.prompt: Which layer of the Earth is liquid metal?

options.text: The outer core
The inner core
options.feedback: The inner core is solid, despite the heat, because of the enormous pressure.

options.text: The mantle
options.feedback: The mantle is solid rock that flows extremely slowly.

options.text: The crust
options.feedback: The crust is solid rock.

items.explain: The liquid iron and nickel of the outer core create the Earth’s magnetic field.

items.prompt: What do most geologists now think mainly drives the plates?

options.text: Slab pull and ridge push
The pull of the Moon’s gravity
options.feedback: Tides move water, not plates.

options.text: The Earth’s spin flinging them outwards
options.feedback: The Earth’s rotation is far too gentle a force to move plates.

options.text: Earthquakes shoving the plates along
options.feedback: Earthquakes are a result of plate movement, not the cause.

items.explain: Older textbooks say convection currents; current thinking puts more weight on dense oceanic plates sinking (slab pull) and new rock pushing out from ridges (ridge push).

items.prompt: At a destructive plate boundary such as the west coast of South America, what happens?

options.text: The oceanic plate sinks under the continental plate
The plates move apart and magma rises to form new crust
options.feedback: That is a constructive boundary.

options.text: The two plates slide past each other sideways
options.feedback: That is a conservative boundary.

options.text: The continental plate sinks under the oceanic plate
options.feedback: The denser plate sinks, and oceanic crust is denser than continental crust.

items.explain: The Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate, building the Andes.

items.prompt: Why is Iceland slowly getting wider?

options.text: Two plates are pulling apart beneath it
Lava drifts across the ocean floor from Hawaii
options.feedback: Hawaii is a hotspot in the Pacific.

options.text: Falling sea levels are uncovering more land
options.feedback: The plates are moving apart, about 2 cm a year.

options.text: Melting glaciers let the land spread outwards
options.feedback: It is plate movement.

items.explain: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through Iceland: the North American and Eurasian plates move apart and magma fills the gap.

items.prompt: The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example of which kind of boundary?

options.text: Conservative: plates slide past
Constructive: plates pull apart
options.feedback: No new crust forms there.

options.text: Destructive: one plate sinks under
options.feedback: No plate sinks there.

options.text: Collision: two continents meet
options.feedback: Collision boundaries build mountain ranges like the Himalayas.

items.explain: No volcanoes, but powerful earthquakes when the stuck plates jerk past each other.

items.prompt: The Himalayas formed where which two plates collide?
distractors: the African and South American plates
the North American and Eurasian plates
items.explain: India is still pushing north, so Everest is still rising by a few millimetres a year.

items.prompt: What is the name for the belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean?
items.explain: About three-quarters of the world’s active volcanoes are in this belt.

items.prompt: On the magnitude scale, how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?

options.text: About 32 times as much
Only a little more: it is one step up
options.feedback: The scale is logarithmic.

options.text: Twice as much
options.feedback: Much more than twice.

options.text: A million times as much
options.feedback: Far too many.

items.explain: Each whole step is about 10 times the ground shaking and about 32 times the energy.

items.prompt: In which year did the Gorkha earthquake (magnitude 7.8) strike Nepal, killing about 9,000 people?
items.explain: It struck on 25 April 2015 and set off avalanches on Everest.

items.prompt: The 2010 Haiti earthquake (magnitude 7.0) killed well over 100,000 people. What was the MAIN reason the death toll was so high?

options.text: Weak, crowded buildings near the epicentre
It was the strongest earthquake ever recorded
options.feedback: Magnitude 7.0 is strong but far from the largest: Chile 1960 was 9.5.

options.text: It struck at night while people slept
options.feedback: It struck just before 5 pm; the weak buildings were the main reason.

options.text: Haiti had never had an earthquake before
options.feedback: Haiti sits near a plate boundary; the issue was vulnerability.

items.explain: The same magnitude kills very different numbers of people depending on buildings, wealth and preparation.

items.prompt: The 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland killed no one. What problem did it cause across Europe?

options.text: Its ash closed European airspace
A tsunami flooded the coast of Norway
options.feedback: There was no tsunami.

options.text: Lava flowed into the North Atlantic
options.feedback: Lava stayed in Iceland.

options.text: It caused the 2010 Haiti earthquake
options.feedback: They are thousands of kilometres apart and unconnected.

items.explain: About 100,000 flights were cancelled: a reminder that hazards have global, economic effects.

items.prompt: About 3,600 years ago, the volcano on Thera (Santorini) erupted. What does the island look like today because of it?

options.text: A ring of islands round a flooded crater
A tall cone-shaped mountain above the sea
options.feedback: The middle of the volcano collapsed into the sea.

options.text: A flat island of black volcanic sand
options.feedback: Its famous cliffs are the caldera walls.

options.text: It sank completely beneath the waves
options.feedback: Much of it survives as a crescent of islands.

items.explain: The Minoan eruption buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri. Some people link it to the legend of Atlantis.

items.prompt: Which of these is a SECONDARY effect of an earthquake?

options.text: Disease from damaged water supplies
Buildings collapsing during the shaking
options.feedback: That happens straight away: a primary effect.

options.text: Gas pipes snapping as the ground moves
options.feedback: That happens at the moment of the quake: a primary effect.

options.text: Roads and bridges cracking apart
options.feedback: Direct damage is primary.

items.explain: Primary effects happen at once; secondary effects follow later as a result: fires, disease, homelessness, lost jobs.

items.prompt: In 2011, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck off Japan. What caused most of the deaths?

options.text: The tsunami that followed it
Buildings falling in Tokyo
options.feedback: Japan’s strict building rules meant most buildings survived the shaking.

options.text: Volcanic eruptions
options.feedback: No eruption was involved.

options.text: A heatwave
options.feedback: It was March.

items.explain: The tsunami swept up to 10 km inland and damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station.

items.prompt: Why do millions of people live near active volcanoes such as Vesuvius?

options.text: Fertile soils, tourism and geothermal energy
They do not know the volcano is still active
options.feedback: Most know very well.

options.text: Volcanoes rarely erupt more than once
options.feedback: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79 and many times since, most recently in 1944.

options.text: The government forbids them to move away
options.feedback: It is a choice, often for good reasons.

items.explain: Benefits and risks are weighed every day by people living with hazards.

items.prompt: What kind of weather does a low-pressure system (a depression) usually bring to the UK?

options.text: Cloud, wind and rain
Clear skies and calm air
options.feedback: That is high pressure.

options.text: Heavy snow, whatever the season
options.feedback: Only if it is cold enough.

options.text: Fog and frost but no wind
options.feedback: Fog and frost come with high pressure in winter.

items.explain: Rising air cools, water vapour condenses into clouds, and rain follows.

items.prompt: Why does high pressure often bring clear skies?

options.text: Air is sinking and warming, so clouds do not form
High pressure pushes clouds away like a broom
options.feedback: It is about sinking air, not pushing.

options.text: The Sun is closer
options.feedback: The Sun’s distance has nothing to do with it.

items.explain: Anticyclones bring sunny summer days and cold, frosty or foggy winter nights.

items.prompt: Why is the west of Britain (e.g. the Lake District) much wetter than the east?

options.text: Relief rain: moist winds rise over the hills
The west is nearer the Equator than the east
options.feedback: They are at similar latitudes.

options.text: The east is too warm for clouds to form
options.feedback: The east is in a rain shadow, but it still has clouds.

options.text: Sea spray from the Atlantic falls as rain
options.feedback: Rain comes from clouds; the key is air rising over the hills.

items.explain: The prevailing wind comes from the south-west, across the warm Atlantic.

items.prompt: Heavy afternoon thunderstorms in the tropics, caused by strong sunshine heating the ground, are an example of which type of rainfall?
items.explain: Hot ground heats the air, which rises fast, cools and forms towering clouds.

items.prompt: Rain caused when warm air rises over a wedge of colder air is called…
items.explain: This happens at the fronts of a depression, which is why UK forecasts show warm and cold fronts.

items.prompt: Why are UK winters much milder than those of places at the same latitude in Canada?

options.text: The warm North Atlantic Drift
The UK is closer to the Sun
options.feedback: Same latitude, same sunlight.

options.text: The UK is lower above sea level
options.feedback: Height is not the reason.

options.text: Cold Arctic air never reaches the UK
options.feedback: Arctic air does reach the UK; the warm ocean current is the difference.

items.explain: This is one reason the UK has a mild, wet maritime climate.

items.prompt: What is a Mediterranean climate like?

options.text: Hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters
Cold winters with snow and cool, wet summers
options.feedback: That is closer to a cold continental climate.

options.text: Hot and wet all year, with daily storms
options.feedback: That is equatorial.

options.text: Hot summers with heavy rain, dry winters
options.feedback: It is the other way round: summers are dry.

items.explain: Greece, southern Italy and southern Spain have it, which is why olives and vines grow so well there.

items.prompt: On a climate graph, how are temperature and rainfall usually shown?

options.text: Temperature as a line, rainfall as bars
Both as pie charts, one per season
options.feedback: Pie charts show proportions, not monthly change.

options.text: Temperature as bars, rainfall as a line
options.feedback: The other way round: bars are for rainfall.

options.text: Rainfall as a line, with no temperature
options.feedback: Both are shown, on two axes.

items.explain: One axis is temperature (°C), the other rainfall (mm).

items.prompt: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?

options.text: Human-made gases trapping extra heat
A hole in the ozone layer letting in heat
options.feedback: The ozone hole is a separate problem (about ultraviolet light).

options.text: Heat escaping from greenhouses and buildings
options.feedback: Real greenhouses are only an analogy.

options.text: The Sun giving out more energy each year
options.feedback: The Sun’s output has not risen enough to explain recent warming.

items.explain: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable; burning fossil fuels has strengthened it.

items.prompt: About how much carbon dioxide was in the air before the Industrial Revolution, in parts per million?
items.explain: Today it is over 420 parts per million: higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years, as ice cores show.

items.prompt: Which of these is EVIDENCE that the climate is changing?

options.text: Ice cores and retreating glaciers
One record-breaking cold winter
options.feedback: A single season is weather, not climate.

options.text: Weather forecasts being wrong more often
options.feedback: Forecast accuracy is not evidence of climate change.

options.text: Rising sales of fans and air conditioners
options.feedback: Sales are not a scientific measurement of climate.

items.explain: Climate is measured over decades; many independent kinds of evidence agree.

items.prompt: Which is a NATURAL cause of climate change?

options.text: Changes in the Earth’s orbit
Burning coal in power stations
options.feedback: Human cause.

options.text: Methane from cattle farming
options.feedback: Human cause (methane).

options.text: Cutting down the rainforests
options.feedback: Human cause.

items.explain: Orbital cycles, volcanic eruptions and changes in the Sun’s output have changed climate in the past.

items.prompt: Which greenhouse gas comes especially from cattle, rice paddies and landfill sites?

options.text: Methane
Oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas.

options.text: Nitrogen
options.feedback: Nitrogen is not a greenhouse gas.

options.text: Helium
options.feedback: Helium is not a greenhouse gas.

items.explain: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, though it lasts less time in the air.

items.prompt: What did countries agree in the 2015 Paris Agreement?

options.text: To keep warming well below 2 °C
To ban all petrol cars by 2020
options.feedback: No such ban was agreed.

options.text: To stop all warming immediately
options.feedback: Some warming is already locked in.

options.text: To stop using all coal by 2016
options.feedback: No such deadline was agreed.

items.explain: Each country sets its own targets and updates them every five years.

items.prompt: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation?

options.text: Mitigation cuts causes; adaptation copes with effects
They are two words for the same response
options.feedback: They are two different responses.

options.text: Mitigation is building sea walls and flood barriers
options.feedback: Sea walls are adaptation.

options.text: Adaptation is planting forests to soak up CO₂
options.feedback: That reduces the cause: mitigation.

items.explain: Good policy needs both.

items.prompt: Which is a likely effect of climate change on the UK?

options.text: Hotter summers and wetter winters
A new ice age within ten years
options.feedback: Not supported by evidence.

options.text: Colder summers and drier winters
options.feedback: Changes are already measured.

options.text: Rain disappearing completely
options.feedback: Winters are expected to get wetter.

items.explain: The UK’s record of 40.3 °C was set at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, in July 2022.

items.prompt: Put these river features in order from source to mouth.
items.explain: Erosion dominates high up; deposition dominates near the sea.

items.prompt: What is hydraulic action?

options.text: Water forcing air into cracks in the bank
Rocks carried by the river scraping the bed
options.feedback: That is abrasion.

options.text: Rocks knocking into each other and breaking
options.feedback: That is attrition.

options.text: Rock dissolving slowly in the water
options.feedback: That is solution.

items.explain: The four erosion processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.

items.prompt: Small pebbles bouncing along a river bed are being transported by…

options.text: saltation
traction
options.feedback: Traction is large boulders rolled along the bed.

options.text: suspension
options.feedback: Suspension is fine particles carried in the water.

options.text: solution
options.feedback: Solution is dissolved minerals.

items.explain: Traction, saltation, suspension and solution: from the heaviest load to the lightest.

items.prompt: Put the formation of an oxbow lake in order.
items: Erosion on the outside of bends makes the meander loop tighter
The neck of the meander narrows
In a flood the river cuts through the neck
Deposition seals off the old loop as an oxbow lake
items.explain: Erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank make meanders migrate until the neck is breached.

items.prompt: Why do waterfalls such as High Force on the River Tees form?

options.text: Soft rock under hard rock erodes faster
A volcano pushes the riverbed up suddenly
options.feedback: No volcano involved.

options.text: People dug them to power water mills
options.feedback: They are natural.

options.text: The sea level dropped suddenly long ago
options.feedback: It is about differences in rock hardness.

items.explain: The hard rock overhang collapses and the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a gorge.

items.prompt: Raised banks of sediment along a river in its lower course, built up by repeated floods, are called…
items.explain: When the river floods, it drops its heaviest sediment first, right beside the channel.

items.prompt: Which of these is SOFT engineering for flood management?

options.text: Planting trees upstream
Building a concrete flood wall
options.feedback: Hard engineering.

options.text: Straightening the river channel
options.feedback: Hard engineering.

options.text: Building a dam and reservoir
options.feedback: Hard engineering.

items.explain: Soft engineering works with natural processes; it is usually cheaper and better for wildlife, but protects less in extreme floods.

items.prompt: Which barrier, completed in 1982, protects London from tidal surges up the Thames?
items.explain: It is closed when a high tide and a storm surge from the North Sea arrive together.

items.prompt: Which statement about the world’s great rivers is correct?

options.text: The Amazon carries the most water
The Thames is the longest in the world
options.feedback: The Thames is about 346 km; the Nile is over 6,600 km.

options.text: The Amazon flows through central Africa
options.feedback: It is in South America.

options.text: The Nile flows south into the Indian Ocean
options.feedback: It flows north into the Mediterranean.

items.explain: Some measurements make the Amazon longer: geographers still argue.

items.prompt: What are destructive waves like?

options.text: Tall and frequent, with a strong backwash that drags material away
Low and gentle, with a strong swash that builds beaches
options.feedback: That describes constructive waves.

options.text: Only found in harbours
options.feedback: They are common in storms everywhere.

items.explain: Destructive waves erode; constructive waves deposit.

items.prompt: Put the erosion of a headland in order.
items.explain: Hydraulic action and abrasion widen a crack into a cave; the cave breaks through as an arch; the arch collapses leaving a stack, which wears down to a stump. Old Harry Rocks in Dorset are famous chalk stacks.

items.prompt: What is longshore drift?

options.text: Waves moving sand along the coast
The tide carrying sand in and out
options.feedback: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon.

options.text: Cliffs slumping into the sea
options.feedback: That is mass movement.

options.text: Wind blowing sand inland into dunes
options.feedback: That builds sand dunes; longshore drift moves sand along the coast.

items.explain: Swash moves material up the beach at an angle with the prevailing wind; backwash pulls it straight back down.

items.prompt: A long ridge of sand or shingle built out into the sea by longshore drift, such as Spurn Head, is called a…
items.explain: Spits form where the coastline changes direction, for example at a river mouth.

items.prompt: The Holderness coast in Yorkshire is eroding by about 2 metres a year. Why so fast?

options.text: Its cliffs are soft boulder clay
Its cliffs are hard granite
options.feedback: Granite is very resistant.

options.text: Quarries are digging the cliffs away
options.feedback: It is natural erosion of soft clay.

options.text: The tides there are unusually high
options.feedback: The tidal range is not the reason: the soft clay is.

items.explain: It is one of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe; villages recorded in the Domesday Book are now under the sea.

items.prompt: What do groynes do?

options.text: Trap sand moving along the beach
Stop the tide coming in too far
options.feedback: Nothing stops the tide.

options.text: Break up waves out at sea
options.feedback: That is an offshore reef or breakwater; groynes run down the beach.

options.text: Hold up the pier and promenade
options.feedback: They are fences down the beach.

items.explain: But they can starve beaches further along the coast of sand, increasing erosion there.

items.prompt: What is managed retreat?

options.text: Letting the sea flood some low land
Building a new sea wall further out to sea
options.feedback: That is advancing the line.

options.text: Moving a whole city inland at once
options.feedback: It is planned, gradual change to the coastline.

options.text: Removing old groynes from the beach
options.feedback: That is not the plan: low land is allowed to flood and become salt marsh.

items.explain: Salt marshes absorb wave energy and are excellent habitats, so managed retreat can be cheaper and greener.

items.prompt: Why might a council decide NOT to protect an eroding stretch of coast?

options.text: The defences cost more than the land is worth
Erosion is impossible to measure accurately
options.feedback: It can be measured precisely.

options.text: The law forbids building any sea walls
options.feedback: Sea walls are allowed.

options.text: Erosion always stops by itself in time
options.feedback: It does not.

items.explain: Cost–benefit analysis is central to shoreline management plans, though it is hard on the people affected.

items.prompt: How does a corrie (also called a cirque or cwm) form?

options.text: Ice in a mountain hollow deepens it
A meteorite strikes a mountainside
options.feedback: Glaciers, not meteorites.

options.text: A mountain stream carves it out
options.feedback: Rivers make V-shaped valleys.

options.text: Strong winds scour it out
options.feedback: Ice is the cause.

items.explain: When the ice melts, many corries hold a small lake called a tarn.

items.prompt: A sharp knife-edge ridge between two corries, such as Striding Edge on Helvellyn, is called an…
items.explain: Where three or more corries meet, a pyramidal peak can form.

items.prompt: How can you tell a valley was carved by a glacier?

options.text: It is U-shaped, with a flat floor and steep sides
It is V-shaped with interlocking spurs
options.feedback: That is a river valley.

options.text: It has a river delta
options.feedback: Deltas form at river mouths.

options.text: It is full of sand dunes
options.feedback: Dunes are coastal or desert landforms.

items.explain: Glaciers fill the whole valley and grind it into a U shape, cutting off spurs.

items.prompt: Long, thin lakes in glacial valleys, such as Windermere, are called…
items.explain: Ice eroded the softer rock of the valley floor more deeply, leaving a long basin.

items.prompt: A boulder carried by ice and dropped far from where it came from is called an…
items.explain: Erratics help geologists track how ice moved.

items.prompt: About how long ago was the last glacial maximum, when ice sheets were largest in Britain?
items.explain: The ice had melted from Britain by about 11,700 years ago.

items.prompt: Put the layers of a tropical rainforest in order, from the top down.
items.explain: Emergents tower above the canopy, which captures most of the light.

items.prompt: Why are tropical rainforest soils surprisingly poor in nutrients?

options.text: Nutrients are locked up in the plants
Hardly any dead leaves fall to the ground
options.feedback: There are plenty, but they decompose very quickly.

options.text: It is too cold for leaves to decompose
options.feedback: It is hot, so decomposition is fast.

options.text: The roots grow on bare rock with no soil
options.feedback: They have soil, just thin and poor.

items.explain: This is why cleared rainforest land often becomes infertile within a few years.

items.prompt: What is the biggest single cause of deforestation in the Amazon?

options.text: Clearing land for cattle ranching
Building theme parks
options.feedback: Not a significant cause.

options.text: Volcanic eruptions
options.feedback: There are no active volcanoes in the Amazon basin.

options.text: Forest fires started by lightning
options.feedback: Most fires there are set by people to clear land.

items.explain: Soya farming, logging, mining and roads matter too.

items.prompt: A hot desert receives less than about how much rain a year?
items.explain: The Sahara is the largest hot desert; some parts get almost no rain for years.

items.prompt: Which is an adaptation of a cactus to the desert?

options.text: Spines instead of leaves
Huge flat leaves to catch sunlight
options.feedback: Big leaves lose too much water.

options.text: Deep roots used only in winter months
options.feedback: Many cactus roots spread widely and shallowly to catch brief rain.

options.text: Bright flowers open all year round
options.feedback: Flowering is brief.

items.explain: Spines also shade the plant and protect its stored water from animals.

items.prompt: Ground in the tundra that stays frozen all year round is called…
items.explain: As it thaws with climate change, it releases methane.

items.prompt: In an ecosystem, what is a producer?

options.text: A plant that makes its own food
An animal that eats only plants
options.feedback: That is a primary consumer.

options.text: A decomposer such as fungi or bacteria
options.feedback: Decomposers break down dead matter.

options.text: The top predator in the food web
options.feedback: Top predators are consumers.

items.explain: All food chains start with producers capturing the Sun’s energy.

items.prompt: Roughly how many people live on Earth today?
items.explain: The world passed 8 billion in 2022, according to the UN.

items.prompt: Put the stages of the demographic transition model in order.
items: high birth rate, high death rate, slow growth
low birth and death rates, stable
death rate higher than birth rate, decline
items.explain: Medicine and clean water cut deaths first; birth rates fall later, as education, contraception and urban living spread.

items.prompt: Japan has an ageing, shrinking population. Which stage of the demographic transition model is it in?

options.text: Stage 5
Stage 1
options.feedback: Stage 1 has very high birth and death rates.

options.text: Stage 2
options.feedback: Stage 2 has rapid growth.

options.text: Stage 3
options.feedback: Japan’s population is now falling, not just slowing.

items.explain: Fewer workers must support more pensioners: a big challenge for health care and the economy.

items.prompt: Which country became the most populous in the world in 2023, according to UN estimates?

options.text: India
China
options.feedback: China was first for decades, but its population is now falling.

options.text: the USA
options.feedback: The USA is third, with about 340 million.

options.text: Nigeria
options.feedback: Nigeria is growing fast but has about 230 million people.

items.explain: Both India and China have more than 1.4 billion people.

items.prompt: Which of these is a PUSH factor for migration?

options.text: War or persecution at home
Better-paid jobs abroad
options.feedback: That pulls people towards a place.

options.text: Good schools in another country
options.feedback: A pull factor.

options.text: Family already living abroad
options.feedback: Usually a pull factor.

items.explain: Push factors drive people away; pull factors attract them.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?

options.text: Refugees flee danger; economic migrants seek work
They are two names for the same people
options.feedback: International law treats them differently.

options.text: Refugees always move to a much richer country
options.feedback: Most refugees live in neighbouring, often poorer, countries.

options.text: Economic migrants are never allowed to move
options.feedback: Many move legally for work.

items.explain: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, refugees have a right to protection.

items.prompt: The number of people per square kilometre is called the population…
items.explain: Distribution is where people live; density is how crowded it is.

items.prompt: A population pyramid has a very wide base and narrow top. What does it suggest?

options.text: A high birth rate and a young population
An ageing population with few young people
options.feedback: An ageing population has a narrow base and wide top.

options.text: A shrinking population with few births
options.feedback: A wide base shows many births.

options.text: Very few people live beyond about 30
options.feedback: It shows fewer older people, not none.

items.explain: Niger’s pyramid looks like this; Japan’s looks almost like an upside-down pyramid.

items.prompt: A city with more than 10 million people is called a…
items.explain: In 1950 there were two megacities; today there are more than thirty.

items.prompt: In about which year did more of the world’s people start living in towns and cities than in the countryside?
items.explain: The UN expects about two-thirds of people to live in urban areas by 2050.

items.prompt: Lagos, in Nigeria, is one of Africa’s largest cities. What drives its rapid growth?

options.text: Rural–urban migration and a high birth rate
People leaving to live in the countryside
options.feedback: That would shrink it.

options.text: It became the capital in 2010
options.feedback: Abuja has been the capital since 1991.

options.text: It has no jobs
options.feedback: It is Nigeria’s business and tech hub, which attracts people.

items.explain: Its growth brings opportunity (jobs, tech start-ups, ports) and challenges (housing, traffic, water, waste).

items.prompt: Dharavi in Mumbai and Makoko in Lagos are informal settlements. What does “informal” mean here?

options.text: Homes built without official permission
A relaxed resort for holidaymakers
options.feedback: Informal means built without official permission, not relaxed.

options.text: Tower blocks built by the government
options.feedback: Those are formal housing.

options.text: Empty land kept for future building
options.feedback: Hundreds of thousands of people live in each.

items.explain: Dharavi has a huge recycling industry and thousands of small businesses: seeing only poverty misses half the story.

items.prompt: London grew enormously in the 1800s. Why?

options.text: Jobs and trade drew people in
The climate became warmer and drier
options.feedback: Climate was not the reason.

options.text: The Romans rebuilt it as their capital
options.feedback: The Romans founded it in about AD 47–50.

options.text: Farming around London became more popular
options.feedback: People left farming for city jobs.

items.explain: London had about 1 million people in 1801 and over 6 million by 1901: the same story megacities tell today.

items.prompt: Which feature makes a city more sustainable?

options.text: Good public transport and green spaces
More motorways leading into the centre
options.feedback: More traffic usually means more pollution.

options.text: Building new homes on all its parks
options.feedback: Green spaces cool cities and reduce flooding.

options.text: Sending all its waste to landfill sites
options.feedback: Recycling is more sustainable.

items.explain: Freiburg in Germany and Curitiba in Brazil are famous examples.

items.prompt: What does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine?

options.text: Life expectancy, education and income
GDP, exports and government debt
options.feedback: HDI was designed to go beyond income alone.

options.text: Population, land area and birth rate
options.feedback: Those are not development measures.

options.text: Numbers of cars, phones and computers
options.feedback: Not part of the HDI.

items.explain: It runs from 0 to 1; Norway, Switzerland and Iceland are usually near the top.

items.prompt: GNI per head means a country’s total income divided by…
items.explain: It is usually given in US dollars so that countries can be compared.

items.prompt: What was the Brandt line (1980)?

options.text: A line between richer and poorer countries
The Equator, redrawn as a policy line
options.feedback: It wiggled: Australia and New Zealand were in the North.

options.text: A railway built across West Germany
options.feedback: Willy Brandt led the report that drew it.

options.text: The Greenwich Meridian through London
options.feedback: That is the Prime Meridian.

items.explain: Today countries such as China, Brazil and the Gulf states have grown so much that the line is far too simple.

items.prompt: Why is the infant mortality rate a useful measure of development?

options.text: It reflects health care, water and food
It shows how many children go to school
options.feedback: That is the school enrolment rate.

options.text: It measures a family’s wealth directly
options.feedback: It is a social measure.

options.text: It counts the babies born each year
options.feedback: That is the birth rate.

items.explain: It is the number of babies per 1,000 born who die before their first birthday.

items.prompt: Which is a PHYSICAL factor that can slow a country’s development?

options.text: Being landlocked
Corruption in the government
options.feedback: That is a political factor.

options.text: High levels of national debt
options.feedback: An economic factor.

options.text: A history of colonial rule
options.feedback: A historical factor.

items.explain: Most uneven development has several causes: physical, economic, political and historical.

items.prompt: Which type of aid is often thought to do most good in the long term?

options.text: Small local projects, such as wells
Emergency food parcels every year
options.feedback: Emergency aid saves lives but does not build long-term change.

options.text: Loans paid back with high interest
options.feedback: Debt can hold development back.

options.text: Huge dams built by foreign firms
options.feedback: Large top-down projects can help, but often miss local needs.

items.explain: Bottom-up projects use appropriate technology that local people can maintain.

items.prompt: What is globalisation?

options.text: Countries becoming more connected
Making accurate maps of the globe
options.feedback: That is cartography.

options.text: Countries joining into one government
options.feedback: There is no single world government; globalisation is about connections.

options.text: The whole planet warming up
options.feedback: Related, but not the definition.

items.explain: Containers, cheap flights and the internet have sped it up enormously since the 1970s.

items.prompt: A company that operates in many countries, such as Apple or Toyota, is called a…
items.explain: TNCs often design products in one country and make them in others where costs are lower.

items.prompt: Why did the shipping container (from the 1950s) transform world trade?

options.text: Standard boxes move between ships and lorries
They made ships faster than planes
options.feedback: Ships are still slower than planes.

options.text: They let goods skip customs checks
options.feedback: Goods still pass through customs.

options.text: They are light enough to fly by air
options.feedback: They are heavy steel boxes, carried by sea.

items.explain: About 90% of the world’s goods travel by sea; Shanghai is the busiest container port.

items.prompt: Which is a DISADVANTAGE when a TNC builds a factory in a lower-income country?

options.text: Profits may go back to the home country
It creates jobs
options.feedback: That is an advantage.

options.text: Local people learn new skills
options.feedback: An advantage.

options.text: Roads and power supplies may be improved
options.feedback: Usually an advantage.

items.explain: The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh led to stronger safety campaigns.

items.prompt: What is Fairtrade?

options.text: A scheme guaranteeing farmers a fair price
Trade with no import taxes at all
options.feedback: That is free trade.

options.text: Buying only from nearby farms
options.feedback: That is buying local; Fairtrade is about prices for farmers.

options.text: A market where prices are fixed by law
options.feedback: Fairtrade is a certification scheme, not a law.

items.explain: It helps producers of coffee, cocoa and bananas, among others.

items.prompt: In 2021 a container ship, the Ever Given, blocked the Suez Canal for six days. Why did it matter worldwide?

options.text: About 12% of world trade uses the canal
It flooded the towns along the canal
options.feedback: No flooding.

options.text: It cut the undersea internet cables
options.feedback: Undersea cables were not affected.

options.text: It stopped Egypt exporting its oil
options.feedback: Supply chains are global.

items.explain: Globalised supply chains are efficient, but fragile.

items.prompt: Which of these is a renewable energy source?

options.text: Wind
Coal
options.feedback: Fossil fuel: non-renewable.

options.text: Natural gas
options.feedback: Fossil fuel.

options.text: Uranium (nuclear)
options.feedback: Nuclear is low-carbon but uranium is not renewable.

items.explain: Renewables: wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal and biomass.

items.prompt: Iceland gets most of its electricity and heating from which two sources?

options.text: Hydro and geothermal
Coal and imported oil
options.feedback: Iceland uses very little fossil fuel for electricity.

options.text: Nuclear and solar
options.feedback: It has no nuclear power stations.

options.text: Wind and tidal power
options.feedback: Its rivers and volcanic heat do most of the work.

items.explain: Its position on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge gives it abundant volcanic heat.

items.prompt: What is one disadvantage of wind power?

options.text: It stops when the wind drops
It gives off carbon dioxide while running
options.feedback: It produces almost none while running.

options.text: The wind will run out one day
options.feedback: Wind is renewable.

options.text: It only works well in deserts
options.feedback: The UK has some of Europe’s best wind.

items.explain: Batteries, pumped storage and links between countries help balance supply.

items.prompt: What is water stress?

options.text: When demand for water exceeds supply
When far too much rain falls at once
options.feedback: That is flooding.

options.text: When rivers flow faster than usual
options.feedback: Fast rivers are not the point: it is about demand and supply.

options.text: When water is too cold to drink safely
options.feedback: Temperature is not the point: it is about demand and supply.

items.explain: Parts of the Middle East use desalination plants to turn seawater into drinking water.

items.prompt: Why do some people try to buy food with fewer “food miles”?

options.text: To cut transport emissions
Local food is always much cheaper
options.feedback: Not always.

options.text: Imported food has fewer vitamins
options.feedback: Freshness varies; the main aim is cutting transport emissions.

options.text: Shops must charge more for it by law
options.feedback: There is no such law.

items.explain: It is not the whole story: food grown in heated greenhouses nearby can have a bigger footprint than food shipped in.

items.prompt: What is a country’s “energy mix”?

options.text: All the sources it gets energy from
Its total energy use per person
options.feedback: That is consumption; the mix is the range of sources.

options.text: Only the oil and gas it produces
options.feedback: It includes every source.

options.text: The weather that affects its energy
options.feedback: Weather affects some sources, but the mix is the sources themselves.

items.explain: The UK’s mix has shifted from coal to gas, wind and other sources; its last coal power station closed in 2024.

items.prompt: Russia is the largest country in the world. About how many time zones does it span?
items.explain: When it is morning in Kaliningrad, it is already evening in Kamchatka.

items.prompt: Which mountain range is traditionally used as the boundary between Europe and Asia in Russia?
items.explain: Most Russians live west of the Urals, in European Russia.

items.prompt: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. About how deep is it?
items.explain: It holds about a fifth of the world’s unfrozen fresh surface water.

items.prompt: How does permafrost affect building in Siberia?

options.text: Nothing at all can be built there

options.text: Buildings sit on heated concrete

items.prompt: The Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok is about how long?

options.text: Tundra, then taiga, then steppe

options.text: Desert, then savanna, then ice

options.text: It has huge reserves of gas and oil

options.text: It has the world’s largest wind farms

options.text: It supplies most of the world’s uranium

items.explain: Pipelines carry Siberian gas thousands of kilometres to customers.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Greece?

items.explain: In myth it is named after King Aegeus, who threw himself into it when he saw black sails on Theseus’s ship.

items.explain: The palace of Knossos on Crete was excavated by Arthur Evans from 1900.

items.prompt: Mira notices that Santorini is packed with cruise passengers in summer. Which is a NEGATIVE impact of mass tourism on small islands?

options.text: More money for local restaurants
options.feedback: A benefit.

items.prompt: What are the “three Ps” of hazard management?

options.text: Prediction, protection and preparation
Plates, pressure and power supplies
options.feedback: Not a framework.

options.text: Planning, policing and payment
options.feedback: Planning is close, but the three Ps are prediction, protection and preparation.

options.text: People, places and emergency plans
options.feedback: Not the standard terms.

items.explain: Predict (monitor), protect (build to resist), prepare (drills, kits, plans).

items.prompt: Which can scientists use to help PREDICT a volcanic eruption?

options.text: Tiny earthquakes and gas
Unusual animal behaviour alone
options.feedback: Animal behaviour is not reliable enough on its own.

options.text: The phase of the Moon and the tides
options.feedback: No reliable link.

options.text: Nothing: eruptions give no warning
options.feedback: Many eruptions give warning signs.

items.explain: Earthquakes still cannot be predicted precisely, but many eruptions can.

items.prompt: Which is an example of PROTECTION against earthquakes?

options.text: Buildings with shock absorbers
An evacuation drill at school
options.feedback: That is preparation.

options.text: A network of seismometers
options.feedback: That is monitoring (prediction).

options.text: Moving away from the coast
options.feedback: That is avoidance, not protection.

items.explain: Tokyo’s tall buildings are designed to sway rather than snap.

items.prompt: Why do lower-income countries often suffer more deaths from similar hazards?

options.text: Less money for strong buildings
Their earthquakes are always bigger
options.feedback: Magnitude does not depend on wealth.

options.text: Their hazards happen more often
options.feedback: Frequency is not the key difference: wealth and preparation are.

options.text: They have more plate boundaries
options.feedback: Wealth, not geology, is the key difference here.

items.explain: Higher-income countries often suffer greater economic losses but fewer deaths.

items.prompt: Every year on 1 September, Japan holds Disaster Prevention Day with drills. This is an example of…

options.text: preparation
prediction
options.feedback: Drills prepare people; they do not predict.

options.text: protection
options.feedback: Protection is about structures.

options.text: mitigation of climate change
options.feedback: Different topic.

items.explain: The date marks the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake.

items.prompt: Hazard risk is often described as hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity to cope. What does “vulnerability” mean?

options.text: How easily people are harmed
How big the earthquake or eruption is
options.feedback: That is the hazard.

options.text: How fast rescue teams arrive
options.feedback: That is capacity to cope.

options.text: How often the hazard happens
options.feedback: That is about the hazard itself, not the people.

items.explain: Reducing vulnerability is often the most effective way to reduce deaths.

items.prompt: Rainfall (mm) for five days: 2, 0, 15, 3, 1. What is the median?
items.explain: Order them: 0, 1, 2, 3, 15. The middle value is 2. (The mean, 4.2, is dragged up by the one wet day.)

items.prompt: Temperatures (°C) on five days: 12, 15, 14, 11, 13. What is the mean?
Populations of four villages: 340, 1,200, 560, 890. What is the range?
items.explain: Range = largest − smallest = 1,200 − 340 = 860.

items.prompt: Why is the interquartile range (IQR) often better than the range?

options.text: Extreme values do not affect it
It is always bigger than the range
options.feedback: It is usually smaller.

options.text: It includes every value equally
options.feedback: It deliberately ignores the top and bottom quarters.

options.text: It is quicker to work out by hand
options.feedback: It is not quicker, and speed is not a statistical reason.

items.explain: IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile.

items.prompt: A scatter graph shows that countries with higher GNI per head tend to have higher life expectancy. This is…

options.text: a positive correlation
a negative correlation
options.feedback: Both go up together, so it is positive.

options.text: no correlation
options.feedback: There is a clear pattern.

options.text: proof that money causes long life
options.feedback: Correlation does not prove causation.

items.explain: Correlation shows a relationship; explaining the cause needs more evidence.

items.prompt: What is a choropleth map?

options.text: Areas shaded by value
A map with contour lines
options.feedback: That is a relief map.

options.text: A map of the ocean floor
options.feedback: That is a bathymetric map.

options.text: Dots placed for each event
options.feedback: It is about shading by value.

items.explain: Use darker shades for higher values, and always include a key.

items.prompt: Kit records the weather on ten days: sun, rain, rain, cloud, rain, sun, cloud, rain, sun, rain. What is the mode?

options.text: rain
sun
options.feedback: Sun appears 3 times; rain 5 times.

options.text: cloud
options.feedback: Cloud appears only twice.

options.text: There is no mode
options.feedback: The most frequent value is rain.

items.explain: The mode is the most common value: the only average that works for categories like this.

items.prompt: The boundary of a drainage basin, usually along high ground, is called the…
items.explain: Rain falling on either side of the watershed ends up in different rivers.

items.prompt: The point where two rivers meet is called a…
items.explain: A tributary is a smaller river that joins the main river at a confluence.

items.prompt: What is infiltration?

options.text: Water soaking into the soil
Water moving through rock deep underground
options.feedback: That is percolation and groundwater flow.

options.text: Water flowing over the surface
options.feedback: That is surface runoff (overland flow).

options.text: Water evaporating
options.feedback: That is an output.

items.explain: Flows: infiltration, percolation, throughflow, surface runoff, groundwater flow.

items.prompt: Match each part of the drainage basin system to its role: precipitation, interception by trees, surface runoff, river discharge into the sea.
items.explain: Inputs enter, stores hold water for a while, flows move it, outputs leave the basin.

items.prompt: On a storm hydrograph, what is the lag time?

options.text: The gap between peak rain and peak flow
How long the storm lasts in total
options.feedback: That is the storm’s duration.

options.text: How long the river stays in flood
options.feedback: Not quite.

options.text: The time until the river level falls again
options.feedback: That is the falling limb, not the lag time.

items.explain: A short lag time means the river rises quickly: a higher flood risk.

items.prompt: Why does an urban area usually have a shorter lag time than a forested area?

options.text: Concrete and drains speed up runoff
Cities get much less rain
options.feedback: They get similar or more.

options.text: Trees make rain fall faster
options.feedback: Trees slow water down by interception.

options.text: Rivers in cities are longer
options.feedback: Length is not the reason.

items.explain: Impermeable surfaces increase runoff; that is why sustainable drainage (SuDS) uses ponds and green roofs.
